measurement.happened:
This week in Italy was dominated by a convergence of political drama, public anger, and institutional upheaval. Here is what unfolded, theme by theme.

PUBLIC ANGER AND THE GENERAL STRIKE: The single most visible event of the week was the general strike that hit Italy on November 20, supported by workers and students across the country. Headlines from Reuters, Bloomberg, and the Financial Times all confirm that thousands took to the streets over wages, public services, and what they see as a government out of touch with ordinary people. The FT framed it as growing anger at Meloni specifically, while Bloomberg noted the protests were aimed at prices and the Meloni budget. This was not a one-off: it followed a week in which the Meloni government simultaneously pushed through an antisemitism law, debated a watered-down exit tax, and celebrated becoming the longest-serving postwar government. The strike crystallized a mood of frustration that had been building. Schools were evacuated after bomb threats on November 21, which the minister attributed to hacker and hoax attacks aimed at destabilizing Italy, though she insisted there was no concrete threat. The combination of a general strike, bomb threats, and a government milestone all landing in the same week gave the impression of a country under strain.

THE DE GENNARO DEATH AND THE MAFIA SHADOW: On November 21, former Italian police chief De Gennaro took his own life while under inquiry connected to the 1992 mafia bombing. Prime Minister Meloni expressed shock. This is a deeply significant event in Italian political and judicial culture. De Gennaro was a towering figure in the fight against organized crime, and his death amid a probe linking to one of Italy's most painful episodes (the 1992 Capaci or Via D'Amelio bombing, depending on which case this refers to) will dominate the national conversation. The Financial Times and Reuters both picked up the story, and the timing, just days after a general strike and a parliament uproar, makes it hard to read as anything other than a moment of national reckoning.

PARLIAMENT AND GOVERNMENT DRAMA: The Meloni government crossed a threshold on November 21, becoming the longest-serving government in postwar Italian history, according to Deutsche Welle. In the same week, parliament commemorated a neo-fascist leader, causing what Reuters described as an uproar. The government also approved an antisemitism law over the objections of leftist opposition, a move that intensified the debate over how criticism of Israel is framed in Italian politics. Lawmakers moved to soften a controversial exit tax after heavy criticism, and the government planned to water down that proposal further. The overall picture is of a government that is consolidating power, pushing through legislation, and absorbing internal and external pressure simultaneously.

THE META FINE AND TECHNOLOGY REGULATION: Italy's competition and consumer authority fined Meta approximately 805 to 887 million euros (the exact figure varies slightly by source) over its access to Android users' photos and videos on Facebook. This was reported by Reuters, the BBC, Deutsche Welle, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, and the Financial Times, making it one of the most widely covered stories of the week. In the same vein, Italy gave the green light to Tesla's assisted driving system ahead of broader EU approval, and the government announced plans to introduce social media curbs for teenagers. The court also delayed a ruling in a Meta and TikTok social media case pending those government curbs. Italy is clearly positioning itself as a regulatory heavyweight in European tech policy.

BANKING AND CORPORATE DEALS: The banking sector was active. Italy leaned toward unconditionally approving Intesa Sanpaolo's bid for Monte dei Paschi di Siena. Germany agreed terms with UniCredit regarding the Commerzbank takeover. CVC abandoned its 3.3 billion dollar acquisition of Italian ingredients maker IRCA. Deutsche Bank's Italian unit was found to have hidden up to 800 million euros in mortgage lending losses. Italian banks overall benefited from interest rate conditions and M&A activity. Webuild completed its takeover of construction group Trevi. The Elkann family lost a bid to exclude evidence in a tax case. The EU signaled that Italy could be freed from deficit disciplinary steps in 2027, a significant fiscal relief. Rothschild and Co anchored Italy at the heart of a European growth plan. Prysmian said it would revisit US dual listing plans.

DEFENSE, SPACE, AND INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMACY: Italy announced a 6 billion euro investment in hybrid-threat defense. Finland's Iceye launched a 2 billion euro bid for Italian rocket maker Avio, but the Italian government gave it a frosty response, and a seized Russia-linked yacht reportedly deterred a bidder for Italy's TISG. China sent its defense minister to Italy for the first time in 18 years, a notable diplomatic signal. Italy pitched Germany for observer status in its fighter jet program. The UK, Australia, Canada, and Italy jointly urged Israel to allow aid into Gaza. Germany and Italy agreed terms on the UniCredit-Commerzbank deal.

THE REVOLUT CASE: An Italian court placed Revolut's Italian unit under supervision over money-laundering failings. The Financial Times provided a detailed account of how Russian money launderers and Italian mobsters put Revolut in the regulatory crosshairs. This is a significant regulatory action against a major fintech player in one of its largest European markets.

SPORTS: Italy was eliminated from the Nations League after being beaten by Belgium, ending a run that had included a loss to Spain as well. Ronaldinho made a winning return to professional football in Italy's third division, a feel-good story that captured attention. A children's football tournament was abandoned due to parents' fighting and abuse. New York Knicks player Josh Hart took a minority stake in an Italian basketball team.

CULTURE AND NATURE: A long-buried ancient library in Rome opened to the public after restoration. A Turner masterpiece returned to Rome. Rome was blanketed in heavy snow, and starlings received an icy welcome in the capital. An Italian hedgehog hospital was profiled in the context of climate change.

IN SUMMARY: Italy this week was a country simultaneously celebrating a government milestone, striking against that same government, mourning a legendary anti-mafia figure, fining a tech giant hundreds of millions of euros, courting Chinese and Finnish investors in defense and space, and arguing about antisemitism, exit taxes, and social media rules. It was a dense, high-pressure week.
measurement.expected:
Looking ahead to the week of November 21 through approximately November 28, 2026, here is what I expect, theme by theme.

THE DE GENNARO AFTERMATH: Almost certain. The suicide of a former police chief amid a 1992 mafia bombing probe will dominate Italian media and political discourse for at least the next five to seven days. Expect Meloni and the opposition to use the event for political positioning. The opposition will press for a full parliamentary inquiry or a special commission. The government will likely call for unity and a period of national mourning. There is a probable chance that new documents or connections to the 1992 bombing will surface in the coming days, either through the court file or through investigative journalism. The emotional weight of this event will overlay everything else happening in the country.

POST-STRIKE POLITICAL PRESSURE: Probable. The general strike of November 20 will not simply evaporate. The unions will likely hold follow-up meetings, issue statements, and possibly organize a second wave of action if the government does not respond to their demands on wages and public services. The Meloni government, which just became the longest-serving in postwar history, will face the awkward task of celebrating that milestone while managing the optics of a country that just struck against it. Expect the government to announce concessions, possibly on the exit tax or on public sector pay, to signal that it has heard the message. The watered-down exit tax proposal is likely to be formally tabled or amended in the coming days.

THE ANTISEMITISM LAW AND SOCIAL MEDIA CURBS: Probable. The antisemitism law, approved over leftist opposition, will face at least one constitutional challenge or a formal appeal from the opposition in the coming days. The social media curbs for teenagers, which the government announced on November 18, will move into the drafting or committee stage. The court delay on the Meta and TikTok case, pending those curbs, means that legal and political timelines are now intertwined. Expect the government to push the curbs through quickly to give the court a framework to rule against, or to use the curbs as a bargaining chip with the opposition.

THE META FINE AND TECH REGULATION: Almost certain. The 805 to 887 million euro fine against Meta will be the subject of legal appeals, industry reactions, and EU-level commentary. Meta will likely file a formal appeal or request a review. The Italian competition authority will issue a detailed public statement justifying the fine. The approval of Tesla's self-driving system will generate follow-up coverage as EU regulators weigh in. The social media curbs will generate a new round of debate among tech companies, parents' groups, and civil liberties advocates.

BANKING AND M&A: Probable. The Intesa Sanpaolo bid for MPS, which Italy is leaning toward approving unconditionally, will move closer to a formal green light or a definitive announcement in the coming week. The UniCredit-Commerzbank deal, with Germany having agreed terms, will enter the next regulatory or shareholder approval phase. The Revolut supervision order will see the company issue a public response and possibly a remediation plan. The Deutsche Bank Italian unit's hidden mortgage losses will generate further scrutiny, possibly from the Bank of Italy or the ECB. Expect at least one new corporate deal or restructuring announcement in the Italian market.

DEFENSE AND SPACE: Possible. The Iceye bid for Avio, which received a frosty response, will either be formally rejected, renegotiated, or trigger a government-led alternative process. The 6 billion euro hybrid-threat defense investment will see the first details of allocation emerge. The Chinese defense minister's visit will generate diplomatic follow-up, possibly a joint statement or a set of bilateral agreements. The Germany-Italy fighter jet program observer status discussion will continue. The TISG bidding process, complicated by the Russia-linked yacht issue, will see either a new round of bids or a government intervention.

EU FISCAL RELIEF: Possible. The EU signal that Italy could be freed from deficit disciplinary steps in 2027 will be the subject of further negotiation and political commentary. The Italian government will likely use this as a selling point domestically to justify its budget priorities. The exit tax softening and the deficit relief together suggest the government is trying to create a more business-friendly environment, and the coming week may see additional fiscal measures announced.

WEATHER AND SEASONAL EVENTS: Probable. Rome's heavy snow of November 21 will be followed by continued cold weather across central and northern Italy. The ski season is about to begin, and the Bloomberg piece about KFC on ski slopes hints at the commercial buildup. Expect transport disruptions, school closures in some areas, and the usual winter weather coverage. The starlings arriving in Rome will be a recurring visual and minor nuisance story.

SPORTS: Possible. With Italy out of the Nations League, the domestic football calendar will continue in Serie A, Serie B, and the third division where Ronaldinho made his return. The Josh Hart investment in an Italian basketball team will generate some follow-up. There is no major international tournament in the immediate window, so sports coverage will be more routine.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES: A parliamentary vote of no confidence triggered by the De Gennaro death or the antisemitism law backlash (possible but would require unusual unity in the opposition). A second, larger wave of protests or a new general strike within the same week (possible if the government is perceived as ignoring the November 20 demands). A sudden escalation in the Revolut case, such as a formal penalty or a withdrawal from the Italian market (possible but would be a big step). A new cyberattack or confirmed hacking incident following the hoax bomb threats (possible, given the minister's warning). An unexpected EU-level ruling or sanction related to Italy's fiscal or trade position (less likely but not impossible given the 2027 deficit relief discussion).

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: A government collapse or early election within this one-week window (the Meloni government just hit a longevity record and has a working majority; a crisis this fast would require a shock beyond De Gennaro). A major natural disaster such as an earthquake or flood (the snow is notable but a full-blown disaster in one week is a stretch). A war or military engagement involving Italy (the defense spending and Chinese visit are significant but do not point to immediate conflict). A currency crisis or sudden lira/euro shock (Italy is in the euro and the fiscal picture, while tense, is not in acute danger). A new pandemic or health emergency (no signals in the headlines). A constitutional referendum or major constitutional change being voted on (the exit tax and antisemitism law are significant but not constitutional in scope).

The suicide of former police chief De Gennaro amid a 1992 mafia bombing probe is a dramatic, emotionally charged event that will define the national mood for the coming days.

The Meloni government became the longest-serving in postwar Italy, pushed through an antisemitism law over opposition, and endured a parliament uproar over a neo-fascist commemoration, making cabinet and parliamentary politics the structural backbone of the week.

delta.motion: Several themes grew sharply between the two photographs. The school bomb threats, which in the first week were a single coordinated hoax hitting 1,800 schools, reappeared on November 21 as a fresh wave that forced evacuations again, but now the minister framed them as hacker and destabilization attacks rather than a one-off prank. The story persisted but shifted from a public-relations crisis into a recurring structural vulnerability. The banking consolidation theme expanded dramatically: in the first week Credit Agricole had merely proposed a BPM merger, but by the second week Italy was leaning toward unconditionally approving Intesa Sanpaolo's bid for Monte dei Paschi, Germany had agreed terms with UniCredit on Commerzbank, CVC had abandoned its 3.3-billion-dollar IRCA deal, and Deutsche Bank's Italian unit was caught hiding 800 million euros in mortgage losses. The banking story went from one proposed deal to a full sector-wide reshuffling. The Meta fine, which was the dominant tech story in week one, stayed roughly the same in scale but was joined by new regulatory actions: Tesla's assisted driving got Italian approval, social-media curbs for teenagers were announced, a court delayed a Meta-TikTok ruling pending those curbs, and Revolut's Italian unit was placed under supervision over money-laundering failings. Tech regulation grew from a single fine into a multi-front regulatory offensive. A major new theme appeared that was absent in the first photograph: the general strike on November 20, the death of former police chief De Gennaro under a mafia-bombing inquiry, parliament's uproar over commemorating a neo-fascist leader, the antisemitism law, and the government becoming the longest-serving postwar administration. These political-drama items collectively form a new dominant cluster. The football theme shrank: Italy went from a dominant 3-1 win over France to elimination from the Nations League after losing to Belgium. The energy and industrial policy theme mostly shrank to background: the Ilva bid, Stellantis-Leapmotor, and gas price cap stories that filled week one did not reappear as headlines in week two, replaced by the 6-billion-euro hybrid-defense investment and the Finland-Iceye bid for Avio. The lighter cultural items (truffle auction, Movember Fiat race, printing-press shop) vanished entirely, replaced by the ancient library reopening, a Turner masterpiece returning, and Rome's heavy snow. The defense and diplomacy theme grew modestly: China's defense minister visiting Italy for the first time in 18 years and the joint UK-Australia-Canada-Italy Gaza aid statement are new entries that were not present in the first photograph.
delta.wind: The expectations were broadly right on the big themes but wrong on the scale and the surprises. The school bomb threats were predicted as almost certain to remain the top domestic story, and they did reappear, but the expectation was of concrete government measures, a cyber-defense unit, and legislative packages. What actually happened was a second wave of evacuations plus a ministerial framing of hacker attacks, without the dedicated unit or email-authentication law that was forecast. The theme persisted but in a thinner, more reactive form than expected. The banking consolidation was predicted as probable with multiple headlines, and that came true in spades, but the expectation centered on the Credit Agricole-BPM deal entering formal negotiation. Instead, the BPM story was overtaken by Intesa's Monte dei Paschi bid, the UniCredit-Commerzbank terms, and the CVC-IRCA collapse. The BPM deal was predicted to be unlikely to be signed within seven days, and it indeed was not the lead story. The expectation missed the breadth of the banking reshuffling. The Meta fine was predicted to generate at least one follow-up headline, and it did, but the expectation did not anticipate the Revolut supervision, the Tesla approval, the teen social-media curbs, or the court delaying the Meta-TikTok ruling. Tech regulation grew far beyond a single-fine follow-up. The Nations League fixture against Belgium was predicted as almost certain, and Italy did play Belgium, but the expectation was of group-table implications and a positive backdrop from the France win. In reality Italy was eliminated, a much sharper outcome than the neutral 'next fixture' framing suggested. The energy and industrial policy theme was rated only possible, and it largely faded, which was roughly in line with the low confidence. The defense and foreign policy theme was rated possible, and it did produce headlines (China's defense minister, the 6-billion-euro defense investment), but the expectation did not foresee the China visit or the Iceye-Avio bid. The credit-rating and fiscal outlook was rated possible as a mention, and the EU signaling that Italy could be freed from deficit disciplinary steps in 2027 is a related but more concrete development than was anticipated. The biggest miss was the cluster of political drama: the general strike, the De Gennaro death, the neo-fascist commemoration uproar, the antisemitism law, and the longest-serving-government milestone were not in the expectation list at all. The expectation treated Meloni's coalition as stable enough to avoid a no-confidence motion, and that held, but the strike and the De Gennaro death created a pressure that the forecast did not model. The expectation also did not foresee the Revolut money-laundering supervision, the EU fiscal-relief signal, or the China defense-minister visit. In summary, the expectations correctly identified the persistent threads (bomb threats, banking, Meta, football) but underestimated the political-emotional temperature, overestimated the specificity of the banking negotiation, and missed several new actors (Revolut, Iceye, China) and one of the week's defining events (the general strike and De Gennaro's death).
delta.driver: The force pushing Italy from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a government that is consolidating institutional power and a public that is losing patience with the cost of living. Meloni's coalition just crossed the threshold into becoming the longest-serving postwar government, which should be a moment of confidence, but the same week brought a general strike, a second wave of school evacuations, a legendary anti-mafia figure dying under a probing inquiry, and a parliament arguing over antisemitism and exit taxes. The underlying driver is fiscal and social strain: the government is trying to balance sovereign-debt stability, attract foreign bank capital, fund a 6-billion-euro defense buildout, and keep power bills down, all while the opposition and the public feel that the benefits are not reaching ordinary workers. The banking consolidation, the Meta fine, the Revolut supervision, and the tech-regulatory push are all expressions of a state that wants to project strength and control in a European context where it has historically been seen as a laggard. The De Gennaro death and the mafia-bombing inquiry tap into Italy's deepest institutional anxieties about accountability and the reach of organized crime. The general strike is the pressure valve for all of it. In short, the driver is a government at its most powerful moment meeting a public at its most restless, with the banking, tech, and defense stories providing the structural backdrop against which that tension plays out.

crystal.reasoning: I start from the present: Italy is in a high-pressure state where a government that just became the longest-serving postwar administration is simultaneously being struck by a general strike, mourning a legendary anti-mafia figure who died under a probing inquiry, arguing in parliament over antisemitism and neo-fascist commemoration, and reshaping its banking and tech-regulatory landscape. The motion tells me three things. First, the political-emotional cluster (strike, De Gennaro, neo-fascist uproar, antisemitism law) is new and dominant, and it will not simply vanish in seven days; it will generate follow-up parliamentary action, opposition statements, and media analysis. Second, the banking consolidation expanded from one deal to a sector-wide reshuffling, and the wind shows I keep underestimating the breadth and overestimating the specificity of any single transaction; the Intesa-MPS deal is 'leaning toward approval' but the CVC-IRCA collapse and Deutsche Bank losses mean the sector story is broader than any one signature. Third, tech regulation went from a single Meta fine to a multi-front offensive (Revolut, Tesla, teen curbs), and the wind says I underestimated Italy's regulatory assertiveness; the court delaying the Meta-TikTok ruling pending the teen curbs means those curbs will be formalized or debated next week. The wind also corrects me in a crucial way: I keep expecting formal, orderly institutional responses (parliamentary questions, cabinet approvals, ministerial briefings) when reality delivers reactive, public-facing, sometimes chaotic moments. The defense minister calling hackers 'idiots' is the model, not the parliamentary committee hearing. So I will weight reactive, public, emotionally charged developments over quiet legislative packages. The De Gennaro death is the single most emotionally resonant event of the week and will anchor the national conversation; the mafia-bombing inquiry connection (1992 Capaci or D'Amelio) will generate intense scrutiny. The opposition will use the strike plus De Gennaro plus the neo-fascist commemoration to build a case that the government is out of touch, and I will expect a formal parliamentary challenge, though not a successful no-confidence vote. The general strike's aftermath will produce a small government concession package and continued union agitation, but a second full strike within seven days is unlikely. The banking story will produce at least one major headline, but I will not bet on a specific deal being signed; I will bet on the sector continuing to churn. The tech-regulatory front will produce a follow-up, likely the formalization of the teen social-media curbs or a new action against a fintech player. The defense and diplomacy thread (6-billion-euro investment, Iceye-Avio, China visit, Gaza statement) will generate moderate follow-up but is unlikely to dominate. I would not bet on: a government collapse, a second general strike, a cabinet reshuffle, a major new cyberattack beyond the school-threats thread, the Intesa-MPS and UniCredit-Commerzbank deals both being formally signed in the same week, or the De Gennaro inquiry producing a major arrest within seven days. The less-likely surprises the motion makes more probable are: the opposition filing a formal no-confidence motion (momentum from the strike and De Gennaro), the EU formally announcing the 2027 deficit relief (the signal was given, the announcement could land), a new tech regulatory action following the pattern, and the Iceye-Avio bid being formally rejected or entering a government-guarantee negotiation. I correct for the wind by weighting the chaotic and reactive over the formal and planned, by expecting new actors to appear that I cannot name, and by keeping my confidence in any single specific outcome at medium or below.

crystal.eli5:
Italy is going through a really intense week. A legendary police chief who spent his whole life fighting the mafia killed himself while he was being investigated about a bombing from 1992 that still hurts the country. On top of that, workers went on a big strike to complain about wages and the government, and parliament got into a loud fight about a law and a neo-fascist figure. All of this is happening to the same government that just became the longest-lasting one since World War II, which makes the tension even more dramatic.

The banking world is also in the middle of a big reshuffle. Several major banks are merging, one deal fell apart, and another bank was caught hiding losses. It's like a giant game of musical chairs where everyone is trying to figure out who owns what, and the government is trying to make sure it doesn't lose control.

On the tech side, Italy has been really aggressive this month, fining Meta hundreds of millions of euros, putting a fintech company under supervision for money-laundering problems, and announcing new rules for teenagers on social media. That energy is not going to stop, so expect more of the same. Schools also got hit by a second wave of fake bomb threats, and the government is now calling them hacker attacks, which means more press conferences and promises to fix things.

The big question for next week is whether the opposition can turn all of this frustration into a real parliamentary challenge. They probably will try. They probably will not succeed. But the fight itself will be the story.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A delivered a detailed, structured picture of the coming week organized around six thematic pillars. Its strongest hits were the Meta fine (which it correctly identified as a landmark enforcement moment generating several days of coverage, though it underestimated the breadth of the story by not anticipating the Tesla green light, the social media curbs for teenagers, the court delay on the Meta/TikTok case, or the Revolut supervision order that all amplified the 'Italy as digital enforcer' theme). It correctly saw the school hoax as a continuing story with parliamentary fallout and the defense minister's colorful language being dissected, though it overestimated the school story's dominance relative to what actually happened. The banking consolidation theme was present but in a different shape: A predicted the Credit Agricole-BPM merger as the central banking narrative, while the actual week featured Intesa Sanpaolo's MPS bid and the UniCredit-Commerzbank terms as the lead stories. judgment.comparison:
Both forecasts were structurally similar and shared the same core instincts: the school hoax would continue, banking consolidation and the tax fight would generate parliamentary tension, the Meta fine would be a major story, football would provide a lighter counterweight, and defense/international affairs would be a background thread. Both got the broad strokes of the week's themes right and both missed the three biggest single events: the general strike, the De Gennaro death, and the Meloni government's postwar longevity milestone. These were largely unpredictable from the prior week's headlines, so the miss is understandable, but it means neither forecast captured the emotional and political texture of the actual week, which was defined by public anger, national mourning, and institutional self-congratulation all colliding.

Where the forecasts diverged was in specificity and calibration. Forecast A was more granular, naming the Amazon-Chinese-goods prosecution, the Ilva Jindal/Arvedi bidding, the Stellantis-Leapmotor cooperation, the Open Fiber refinancing, the Enel data-center plan, and the UK-Scotland hoax connection. Most of those specific items did not generate headlines this week, so A's extra detail was a net negative in terms of hits versus misses. Forecast B was somewhat less granular but made a few more precise calls that landed: it correctly identified Belgium as the next Nations League opponent (A just said 'Serie A will resume'), it mentioned the Movember Fiat 500 challenge (which did conclude), and it referenced the Pumas rugby win (a smaller but real story). B's confidence tiers were also slightly better calibrated: by marking the school story as 'almost certain' rather than 'the dominant story,' it avoided the overcommitment that A made, and by marking defense as 'possible but unlikely to be a lead story,' it was closer to the truth than A's 'low-to-medium confidence' framing, even though both undersold the actual defense coverage.

The Meta fine story was a clear hit for both, but the actual week's tech-regulation coverage was broader than either forecast anticipated, extending to Tesla, social media curbs for teenagers, the court delay on the Meta/TikTok case, and the Revolut supervision order. Neither forecast named Revolut, which was a notable omission given the Financial Times' detailed reporting on Russian money launderers and Italian mobsters. The banking story was present in both forecasts but the actual week's lead banking headlines (Intesa-MPS, UniCredit-Commerzbank, Deutsche Bank's hidden losses, CVC abandoning IRCA) were a different mix than either predicted, with the Credit Agricole-BPM proposal being less prominent than both A and B expected.

The general strike was the week's most visible event and neither forecast mentioned it. Both noted the political tension around Meloni, the opposition's attacks, and the government's legislative push, but neither connected those threads to a country-wide walkout. This is the single biggest shared miss. The De Gennaro death was a genuine surprise that neither could have reasonably predicted from the prior week's headlines, though it became one of the most discussed stories. The Chinese defense minister's visit was another genuine surprise that both missed, though A's and B's defense sections at least acknowledged the fighter-jet thread and the Red Sea question, so the broader defense theme was on their radar even if the specific event was not.

In terms of serving a reader, both forecasts would have given a reasonable sense of the threads to watch. A reader following A would have been well prepared for the Meta fine, the school hoax, the banking/tax debate, Ronaldinho, and the fighter-jet story, but would have been blindsided by the strike, De Gennaro, the government milestone, the Chinese visit, and the Revolut story. A reader following B would have had a similar experience, with the slight advantage of knowing Belgium was the next opponent and the Fiat challenge was in the running, and the slight disadvantage of B's somewhat vaguer treatment of the banking specifics. Neither forecast would have made a reader feel they had a complete picture of the week that actually unfolded, because the week's defining events were largely new developments rather than continuations of existing threads.

On balance, the two forecasts are very close in quality. A's greater specificity gave it more opportunities to be wrong on details that did not materialize, while B's slightly more cautious framing and a few more precise small calls (Belgium, Fiat challenge) gave it a marginal edge in accuracy per unit of prediction. But the difference is small, and both shared the same major blind spots. I would give B a very slight edge for better calibration and a few more small hits, but this is close to even.

VERDICT: B
